objective: Prove: (1) for the parity law on a doubly periodic plane graph G (one parity knot per vertex, variables on edges; G and its dual G* locally finite and 2-connected), bond distance is twice the graph distance of G* up to o(|x|), so the circle is half the velocity polygon of G*, a centrally symmetric polygon with rational vertices in lattice coordinates, and its Golab self-perimeter pi is rational in [3, 4]; (2) by Niven's theorem the only affinely regular circles of periodic laws are parallelograms (pi = 4) and hexagons (pi = 3), so no periodic law has a round circle; (3) for the law with one parity knot at each crossing of a simple arrangement of lines in k directions with densities rho_j and bounded gaps, bond distance is 2 sum_j rho_j |<x, n_j>| + O(1), so the circle is the polar of a zonotope; n equiangular equally dense families give a regular 2n-gon with pi = 2n sin(pi/2n) (n odd) or 2n tan(pi/2n) (n even), periodic only for n = 2, 3; the pentagrid (Penrose) law has pi = 5/phi. Compute the exact circle and pi of the parity laws on the 11 Archimedean and 11 Laves tilings and check bond distances against the polygons by exact minimum cycles on large patches.
status: Proved (LOGIC-CIRCLE-20261107-001A-P001): circles of periodic laws are polygons. For the parity law on a doubly periodic plane graph, bond distance is twice the dual's graph distance up to a constant, so the circle is half the dual's velocity polygon, with rational vertices; its pi (Golab's half self-perimeter) is rational in [3, 4], and by Niven's theorem the only regular circles are parallelograms (pi = 4) and hexagons (pi = 3). On line arrangements, bond distance is twice the number of separating lines plus O(1): n equiangular families give a regular 2n-gon with Archimedes' pi, 2n sin(pi/2n) or 2n tan(pi/2n), irrational for n >= 4 and periodic only for n = 2, 3; the Penrose pentagrid law has pi = 5/phi. Exact table: the 19 laws on Archimedean and Laves tilings have pi in {3, 10/3, 16/5, 7/2, 11/3, 4}.
title: Polygons: the circle of a periodic or line-arrangement law and its pi
